# Porcelain (`porcelain`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/materials.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Metallurgy & materials (`materials`)
- Deps: needs fired_brick_ceramics; helped by refractories_fireclay
- Core idea: A traditional Jingdezhen hard-paste porcelain body combines kaolin, a white clay that does not melt, and china stone (a feldspar-rich rock, ground fine), which melts and binds it. Roughly equal parts are shaped, usually glazed with china stone mixed with lime or ash, and fired at 1280–1400 °C in a kiln that can hold that heat for a day, with a smoky, air-starved flame at the peak so that traces of iron do not turn it yellow. The body becomes white, dense, ringing and translucent where thin. The ware is stacked in fireclay boxes (saggars) to keep off ash and flame.
- Pitfalls:
  - Confusing ceramic bodies: some European soft-paste porcelains use glass frit, while bone china uses calcined bone ash with clay and a flux. Their firing behaviour differs from hard paste.
  - Believing the old tales that it is made from eggshells or shells buried for a century.
  - A common pottery kiln stops near 1000–1100 °C; porcelain needs a different kiln and firebricks.
  - Any iron in the clay or water spots the ware; kaolin deposits must be sought (Saxony, Cornwall, Limoges).
- History: china: c. 1600 BC high-fired 'proto-porcelain'; c. 2nd c. AD Eastern Han porcelain in Zhejiang; c. 600 white porcelain (Xing ware); from c. 1000 Jingdezhen; 14th c. blue-and-white; east_asia: c. 10th c. Korea (celadon, then white porcelain); 1616 Arita, Japan, by tradition founded by Korean potters; islamic: 9th c. tin-glazed imitations in Iraq; 11th–12th c. stonepaste (fritware) bodies in Egypt and Iran; europe: 1575–1587 Medici soft-paste porcelain, Florence; 1708 Tschirnhaus and Böttger make hard-paste porcelain in Saxony, Meissen factory 1710; 1712 and 1722 letters of Père d'Entrecolles describe Jingdezhen
- Read:
  - Rose Kerr & Nigel Wood, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 5 part 12: Ceramic Technology (2004)
  - Janet Gleeson, The Arcanum: The Extraordinary True Story (1998)
